intro: Two students answered the same Section C question in fifteen minutes. One scored 4 out of 8, the other 7. Decide which is which and why, before you see the marks. The exam rubric has four parts, analysis 3, knowledge 2, structure 1, writing 2, and markers read for the same things every time; once you can spot them in someone else's answer you will put them in your own.
checklist: A contention in the first sentence that answers the question (structure)
Specific, accurate evidence from class, with dates, names or places (knowledge)
A because sentence after each piece of evidence that links it to the argument (analysis)
Shows how one impact or factor led to another, and names historical significance (analysis)
A final sentence that returns to the question with a judgement (structure and analysis)

pairs.q: Analyse the impact of the feudal system on medieval Europe.

weak.text: [[The feudal system was the way medieval Europe was organised.||First sentence names the topic but makes no judgement. There is no contention to argue for.]] At the top was the king, who owned all the land. He gave land to the barons in return for loyalty and soldiers. The barons gave land to knights, who promised to fight for them for forty days a year. At the bottom were the peasants, who worked the land and gave food to the lord. Serfs were not allowed to leave the manor without permission. [[The feudal system had a big impact because everyone had a place and knew their job.||'Big impact' is not analysis. Which impact? On whom? Compared with what?]] It also meant the king could get an army without paying for one. The Church was also part of the feudal system because it owned a lot of land. [[The feudal system started to end after the Black Death because there were not enough workers.||The one cause-and-effect sentence in the answer, and it is accurate. No date, no law, no event, so it earns a knowledge mark but not an evidence mark.]] [[Overall the feudal system had a big impact on medieval Europe because it affected everyone from the king to the peasants.||The conclusion repeats the question. 'Affected everyone' is true of almost anything and weighs nothing.]]
weak.why: Analysis 1: it describes how the system worked rather than analysing what it did, and nothing connects to anything else. Knowledge 1: accurate but without a single date, and the facts support no argument. Structure 1: it has an opening and a closing sentence. Writing 1: plain and repetitive.

strong.text: [[The feudal system's greatest impact on medieval Europe was political: it gave kings a way to control a kingdom without a paid army, and that control shaped everything else.||Contention in the first sentence. It answers the question and takes a position ('greatest impact was political') that the rest of the answer has to defend.]] After 1066 William granted England's land to about 180 barons in return for oaths of loyalty and knight service, and [[the Domesday Book of 1086 recorded every holding so the king knew exactly what he was owed.||Dated, specific evidence, and the 'so' clause explains why it matters to the argument.]] This mattered because power now came from land, so a lord who broke his oath could lose everything. Second, feudalism fixed the lives of ordinary people. [[On the manor a serf worked the lord's own fields, paid rent in produce, and needed permission to marry or leave; for a peasant family the system decided where they lived, what they ate and who judged them.||This is the 'so what for people' step. It names a group and says what the system meant for them day to day.]] However, the system's weakness shows its significance just as clearly. [[When the Black Death of 1347 killed around a third of the population, surviving labourers could demand wages, the Statute of Labourers in 1351 tried to freeze them, and anger at that law fed the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.||Three dated events linked in a chain: cause, response, consequence. This is cause and effect shown, not just named.]] [[The feudal system therefore mattered most as a political structure, because when the land-for-service bargain stopped working, the whole order began to break.||Returns to the contention and gives a reason for the judgement.]]
strong.why: Knowledge 2, structure 1, writing 2. Analysis 2 rather than 3: the answer explains a chain (plague, labour shortage, the 1351 law, the 1381 revolt) and names significance, but the final claim that the political impact mattered most is asserted rather than argued against the social impact the answer itself described, so the links between the points are uneven. Sustain the connection to the end and it is an 8.

pairs.q: Analyse how the Tokugawa shogunate kept control of Japan for over 250 years.

weak.text: The Tokugawa shogunate ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868. [[They kept control in lots of ways.||'Lots of ways' is a list announcement, not a contention. The question asks how; a strong answer says which method mattered most.]] [[First, there was sankin kotai, which meant the daimyo had to live in Edo every second year and leave their families there. Second, the Laws for the Military Houses told the daimyo what they could and couldn't do, like building castles. Third, there was the four-class system with samurai at the top, then peasants, artisans and merchants. Fourth, Japan was closed to the world under sakoku so foreign ideas couldn't come in.||Four methods, each named correctly, none explained. Not one 'because' sentence says how the method stopped rebellion.]] Christianity was banned. [[The shogunate also had sword hunts so peasants couldn't have weapons.||A slip. The sword hunt was Hideyoshi's, in 1588, before the Tokugawa. Markers notice.]] [[These things all helped the Tokugawa keep control because the daimyo were watched and the peasants couldn't rebel.||The only explanation in the answer, and it covers all six methods in one sentence.]] [[That is how the Tokugawa kept control for over 250 years.||Restates the question.]]
weak.why: Analysis 1: a list of policies with one sentence of explanation covering all of them, so no relationships between factors are shown. Knowledge 1: five real Tokugawa policies (the sword hunt is Hideyoshi's), but they are named, not used to support an argument. Structure 1: opening and closing sentences. Writing 1: 'First, second, third' is a list, not an argument.

strong.text: [[The Tokugawa kept control for more than 250 years mainly by making rebellion by the daimyo impossible, and only secondly by controlling everyone else.||Contention that answers the question and gives the answer a shape: daimyo first, everyone else second.]] The most important tool was sankin kotai, made compulsory in 1635. Every daimyo had to spend alternate years in Edo and leave his wife and heir there permanently. [[This worked in two ways at once: the family was a hostage, and the cost of the processions and two households drained the money a daimyo would have needed for an army.||Explains the mechanism. This is the difference between naming sankin kotai and analysing it.]] The Buke Shohatto of 1615 backed this up by banning new castles and unapproved marriages, [[so the alliances that had torn Japan apart in the century of civil war after 1467 could not form again.||Links the law to a real earlier problem. Shows the student knows why the rule existed.]] Control of ordinary people came second. The four-class system fixed a person's occupation at birth, and sakoku, complete by 1639, cut off the foreign guns and Christian ideas that had unsettled the 1500s. [[For a peasant this meant a lifetime in one village paying rice tax; for a merchant it meant wealth without status.||Two groups, two different experiences of the same system. Perspectives, shown rather than named.]] [[Because the daimyo were the only group with the men and money to overthrow a shogun, the policies aimed at them were the ones that mattered most,||Judgement with a reason, which is where the concept of significance belongs; the idea is here, the word is not.]] which is why the shogunate only fell when outside pressure from Perry in 1853 exposed its weakness.
strong.why: Knowledge 2, structure 1, writing 2. Analysis 2 rather than 3: the mechanisms are explained and connected, but the Perry point at the end is a strong idea dropped in half a sentence, and the word significance never appears although the idea is there. Develop the ending and name the concept, and it is an 8.

pairs.q: Analyse the influence of the Catholic Church on medieval European society.

weak.text: [[The Catholic Church was very powerful in medieval Europe.||'Very powerful' is a description, not a contention. Powerful in which way, and which way mattered most?]] Everyone was Catholic and went to church. The Church controlled people's lives from birth to death because it did baptisms, weddings and funerals. People had to pay a tithe which was ten percent of what they earned. The Church was also very rich and owned lots of land. Monks lived in monasteries and copied books. [[The Pope was the head of the Church and was even more powerful than kings. He even excommunicated King John in 1209.||A date and a name, which is why this is a 4 and not a 3. But the example is dropped in without saying what happened next or why it mattered.]] People believed that if they did not obey the Church they would go to hell. The Church also started the Crusades. [[In conclusion the Church had a huge influence on medieval society because it controlled religion, money and politics.||Three areas listed, none ranked. The conclusion is a summary, not a judgement.]]
weak.why: Analysis 1: true statements about the Church with no explanation of how any of them shaped society. Knowledge 1: one dated example, dropped in and not used. Structure 1: a conclusion that lists three areas. Writing 1: short, repetitive sentences.

strong.text: [[The Church's deepest influence on medieval society was over ordinary people's daily lives, more than its famous power over kings.||A contention that takes a side. It will have to show both kinds of influence and then rank them.]] From baptism to burial, every villager's life ran through the parish church: the year was organised around holy days, the priest was often the only person who could read, and [[doom paintings on the church wall showed exactly what disobedience would cost.||Specific, visual evidence with a purpose attached.]] The tithe, a tenth of every harvest, made the Church the largest landowner in England, holding roughly a quarter of the land. [[For a peasant family this was not abstract: the Church decided when they rested, who they could marry and where their grain went.||'So what for people', done in one sentence.]] The Church's political power was real but less constant. [[When Pope Innocent III excommunicated King John in 1209 and placed England under interdict, closing every church for six years and John eventually gave way, showing that even a king depended on the Church's approval.||Dated example, explained. This is what the weak answer's 'more powerful than kings' needed.]] [[However, that was a dramatic exception, whereas the control of village life was permanent.||The sentence that connects the two kinds of influence. 'However' and 'whereas' do the analytical work.]] The Church therefore shaped medieval society most through the everyday, because its hold on belief and the calendar reached every person, every week, for centuries.
strong.why: Knowledge 2, structure 1, writing 2. Analysis 2 rather than 3: both kinds of influence are explained and connected to people's lives, but the claim that political power was less constant rests on a single example, and the answer never says whether the Church's influence changed across the period. One more connected example and it is an 8.

pairs.q: Analyse the significance of sakoku for Japan.

weak.text: Sakoku means closed country. It was introduced by the Tokugawa shogunate in the 1630s. Under sakoku Japanese people were not allowed to leave Japan and foreigners were not allowed to come in. [[The only country allowed to trade was the Dutch, on the island of Dejima in Nagasaki, and also China.||Correct and specific, but it contradicts 'foreigners were not allowed to come in' without explaining the contradiction. A strong answer uses Dejima to show that sakoku was control, not total closure.]] Christianity was banned and people who were Christians were killed. [[Sakoku was significant because Japan was cut off from the world for over 200 years.||The first 'significant because'. Being cut off is what sakoku was, not what it did.]] This meant Japan did not get new technology like steam ships. When Commodore Perry came in 1853 Japan could not fight back. [[Sakoku was also significant because it kept Japan peaceful.||The best idea in the answer, given one sentence and no evidence. This is where the marks were.]] [[So sakoku was very significant for Japan.||Restates the question with 'very' added.]]
weak.why: Analysis 1: two significances are stated, not explained, and nobody in Japan is mentioned, so no perspectives and no connections. Knowledge 1: accurate description, one date. Structure 1: opening and closing sentence. Writing 1: 'very significant' is doing the work analysis should.

strong.text: [[Sakoku was significant less for what it stopped than for what it allowed: two centuries of peace that changed how Japanese people lived, at the price of military weakness that ended the shogunate.||Contention that sets up both arguments and the judgement between them in one sentence.]] The edicts of 1635 to 1639 banned Japanese from leaving, expelled the Portuguese, and limited foreign contact to the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki, [[where Dejima let the shogun control exactly what came in.||Same fact as the weak answer, but explained: Dejima shows sakoku was about control.]] With no foreign wars and no daimyo alliances with outside powers, the peace held. [[Samurai became officials rather than fighters; Edo grew past a million people by 1700; merchants grew rich trading rice while their status stayed at the bottom.||Three groups, each with a changed experience. This is the 'so what for people' step.]] This is why the Edo period produced kabuki, woodblock prints and widespread literacy. However, the same isolation meant Japan missed the industrial changes of the 1700s. [[When Perry's steamships arrived in 1853, Japan had no navy that could answer them, and the humiliation of the 1854 treaty turned samurai against the shogunate within fifteen years.||Dated cause-and-effect chain with the people who reacted named.]] [[Sakoku was therefore most significant as a cause of both the stability of the Edo period and the shock that ended it;||Judgement that holds both arguments together rather than picking one and dropping the other.]] its effects reached from the merchant in Osaka to the daimyo who finally turned on the Tokugawa.
strong.why: Knowledge 2, structure 1, writing 2. Analysis 2 rather than 3: the chain from isolation to 1853 is explained and significance is named, but the cultural evidence (kabuki, prints, literacy) is a list with no because linking it to peace, so one link in the argument is missing. Connect it and it is an 8.

pairs.q: Analyse the impact of the Meiji Restoration on Japan.

weak.text: The Meiji Restoration happened in 1868 when the emperor took power back from the shogun. [[It had a big impact on Japan.||No judgement. Which impact, on whom, and compared with what?]] Japan became modern very quickly. [[They built railways and factories and telegraphs. They got a new army with conscription so every man had to serve. The samurai lost their special rights and were not allowed to carry swords. Japan copied the West, with Western clothes and a Western-style constitution in 1889. Japan also sent people overseas to learn. The four class system was ended.||Seven changes in six sentences. All accurate, one dated. None explained, none linked to each other, nobody's experience described.]] [[The Meiji Restoration had a massive impact because Japan went from a feudal country to a modern country in only a few decades and later beat Russia in a war.||The conclusion finally makes a point (speed of change) but proves it with an event from outside the unit, dropped in without explanation.]]
weak.why: Analysis 1: seven changes listed, none explained or connected, no sense that different people experienced them differently. Knowledge 1: accurate and two dates, but the facts support no argument. Structure 1: an opening and a conclusion. Writing 1: 'big' and 'massive' instead of explanation.

strong.text: [[The Meiji Restoration's greatest impact was on who held power and status in Japan, because the political change of 1868 made every other change possible.||Contention with a reason attached.]] Once the emperor replaced the shogun, the new government abolished the domains in 1871 and replaced daimyo with appointed governors, [[ending the land-for-loyalty system that had organised Japan since the 1100s.||Links the change back across the whole unit. Continuity and change, shown.]] [[The samurai lost most: conscription in 1873 meant commoners now filled the army, the sword ban of 1876 removed their visible status, and their rice stipends were converted to bonds.||A group, three dated changes, and what each one took from them.]] Some rebelled, most famously in 1877, and were crushed by the conscript army, [[which proved the change was permanent.||Uses the rebellion as evidence for the argument rather than just mentioning it.]] [[For commoners the impact was mixed. Compulsory schooling and the end of the class system opened careers that had been closed for 250 years, but new land taxes and factory work in places like the Tomioka silk mill were harsh, especially for young women.||Perspectives: a second group, and a balanced view of their experience.]] Modernisation itself, the railways, telegraphs and the 1889 constitution, mattered, but these were tools; the decisive change was that a warrior class that had ruled for seven centuries was dismantled in under ten years. [[The Restoration therefore mattered most as a transfer of power, and its effects were felt very differently depending on who you were.||Judgement that returns to the contention and names the perspectives idea.]]
strong.why: Knowledge 2, structure 1, writing 2. Analysis 2 rather than 3: two groups' experiences are explained and the rebellion is used as proof, but the dismissal of modernisation as 'tools' is asserted in half a sentence and the concept of significance is implied rather than named. Take the counter-case seriously for one sentence and it is an 8.

pairs.q: Analyse the significance of the Crusades for medieval Europe.

weak.text: The Crusades were wars between Christians and Muslims over the Holy Land. They started in 1095 when the Pope said that anyone who went would have their sins forgiven. The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099. [[There were many more crusades but they mostly failed and Jerusalem was taken back by Saladin.||Accurate but undated. 1187 is the kind of date that turns a statement into evidence.]] [[The Crusades were significant because many people died.||True of every war. Not a significance for medieval Europe.]] They were also significant because they brought back new things to Europe like spices, sugar and new knowledge. Castles got better. The Crusades also made the Pope more powerful. [[Overall the Crusades were very significant for medieval Europe because they changed trade, religion and warfare.||Three areas named in the last sentence, none developed in the body, none ranked.]]
weak.why: Analysis 1: 'significant because' three times without any effect explained, so the concept is named but not used. Knowledge 1: two correct dates and a spread of effects, each in one sentence. Structure 1: opening and closing. Writing 1: plain and repetitive.

strong.text: [[The Crusades mattered most for medieval Europe not as a military success, since they failed, but for the contact and trade they forced open.||Contention that already weighs: military failure against long-term exchange.]] When Urban II called the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095, he offered forgiveness of sins, and the capture of Jerusalem in 1099 seemed to prove God's favour. [[Yet Saladin retook the city in 1187 and the last crusader city, Acre, fell in 1291, so in their own terms the Crusades were a two-century defeat.||Dated evidence with a 'so' that draws the conclusion.]] Their lasting significance was elsewhere. [[Venice and Genoa built trading posts across the eastern Mediterranean, and sugar, spices, silk and paper became regular imports; a merchant in Venice gained far more than any knight.||Names who gained. The comparison with the knight is the 'so what for people' step.]] Contact with Islamic scholarship brought medical texts and the lost works of Greek thinkers like Aristotle into European universities. [[The Church gained prestige at first, but the sack of Christian Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade in 1204 showed how far crusading had drifted from its purpose, and the failures weakened the Pope's claim to lead all Christians.||Change over time within one argument: rose, then fell, with a dated turning point.]] [[The Crusades were therefore significant mainly for the long-term exchange of goods and ideas, which outlasted every kingdom the crusaders founded.||Judgement that returns to the contention with a reason.]]
strong.why: Knowledge 2, structure 1, writing 2. Analysis 2 rather than 3: the failure and the long-term exchange are connected and significance is named, but the effect on ordinary Europeans who never went east is missing, so the perspectives are narrow. One sentence on how the Crusades reached the village as well as the merchant and it is an 8.

caveat: Marks here are what a marker would most likely give against the exam rubric. Marking is a judgement within bands, so two markers can differ by a mark on the same answer. There is no formula; the notes show where the marks are usually won and lost.
